lessons.title: Course Introduction: Becoming an Azure Database Administrator
SQL Server On-Prem vs. Azure SQL — Understanding the Ecosystem

slots.practicalActivity: Research and compare, in your own words, on-prem SQL Server vs. Azure SQL (Database, Managed Instance, and SQL Server on an Azure VM) using the official Azure SQL documentation; then sign in to (or create) a free Azure account and open the Azure Portal's 'Create a resource' search bar to confirm you can see all three SQL deployment options listed.
slots.deliverable: A comparison table (on-prem SQL Server vs. Azure SQL Database vs. Managed Instance vs. SQL Server on Azure VM) covering management overhead and control, plus confirmation that you located all three options in the Portal.

lessons.title: Azure SQL Database vs. Managed Instance vs. SQL Server on Azure VM
IaaS vs. PaaS for SQL Server

slots.practicalActivity: Using the Azure Portal's 'Create SQL Database' wizard, step through (without finishing deployment) the three resource-type tabs — SQL databases, SQL managed instances, and SQL virtual machines — noting which configuration options each tab exposes; then write a one-paragraph recommendation for a 50GB OLTP app with a small team and no patching staff, justifying IaaS vs. PaaS.
slots.deliverable: Written notes on what each of the three SQL deployment wizards exposes, plus a one-paragraph IaaS-vs-PaaS recommendation for the given scenario.

lessons.title: Azure Portal, SSMS & Azure Data Studio for DBAs

slots.practicalActivity: Install (or confirm you already have) SQL Server Management Studio and Azure Data Studio; open both and confirm they can each connect to a SQL Server instance, noting in your own words one task you'd rather do in each tool.
slots.deliverable: A note confirming both SSMS and Azure Data Studio are installed and working, with one task you'd prefer to use each tool for.

lessons.title: Lab: Build Your First Azure SQL Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Complete the chapter's hands-on lab: in the Azure Portal, create a resource group rg-dba-course, deploy a new Azure SQL single database inside it using the 'Sample (AdventureWorksLT)' data source option, set a SQL authentication admin login, add your client IP to the server firewall, then connect to it from SSMS and run SELECT TOP 10 * FROM SalesLT.Customer to confirm the sample data loaded.
slots.deliverable: A live Azure SQL Database (AdventureWorksLT sample) inside rg-dba-course, connected successfully from SSMS, with a working SELECT TOP 10 query against SalesLT.Customer.

lessons.title: Azure SQL Purchasing Models, Service Tiers & Compute Options

slots.practicalActivity: In rg-dba-course, create a second Azure SQL server and an additional database from the Portal's 'Create SQL Database' wizard, stepping through every purchasing-model and service-tier option (DTU-based Basic/Standard/Premium vs. vCore-based General Purpose/Business Critical/Hyperscale) without necessarily deploying the most expensive tier; record what compute/storage options each tier exposes.
slots.deliverable: A written comparison table of the purchasing models and service tiers seen in the wizard, plus a second deployed database at a tier you chose and justified in one sentence.

lessons.title: DTU vs. vCore & Choosing the Right Database Configuration

slots.practicalActivity: On your second database, open Compute + storage in the Portal and toggle between a DTU-based tier and a vCore-based tier to compare the sliders and price estimates for the same workload; then create an elastic pool in the Portal, add both of your databases to it, and compare the pool's shared eDTU/vCore allocation against what each database used standalone.
slots.deliverable: Notes comparing DTU vs. vCore slider options for the same workload, plus an elastic pool containing both databases with its shared compute allocation recorded.

slots.practicalActivity: On the AdventureWorksLT database from Chapter 1's lab, open the Portal's Compute + storage blade and increase the max storage size by one increment, then use Query Performance Insight to see how the database's resource consumption (DTU/vCore percentage) looked before and after the change.
slots.deliverable: A before/after screenshot or note from Query Performance Insight showing resource consumption, plus confirmation the storage size change was applied.

lessons.title: Azure SQL Managed Instance Deployment & Configuration

slots.practicalActivity: In the Portal, step through the 'Create Azure SQL Managed Instance' wizard's network and compute configuration screens (without necessarily completing the multi-hour deployment) to see what a Managed Instance requires — a dedicated subnet, for example — that a single database does not; write a note on the 3 biggest configuration differences versus this chapter's single-database deployments.
slots.deliverable: A written note listing the 3 biggest configuration differences between deploying a Managed Instance and deploying a single Azure SQL Database.

lessons.title: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines & Hybrid SQL

slots.practicalActivity: In the Portal, start the 'Create a Virtual Machine' wizard and select a SQL Server image from the Marketplace (e.g. SQL Server 2022 on Windows Server), stepping through the VM size and SQL Server settings tabs to see which licensing and connectivity options appear that don't exist for PaaS options; write a one-paragraph recommendation for when you'd choose a SQL Server VM over Managed Instance.
slots.deliverable: A one-paragraph written recommendation on when a SQL Server-on-VM deployment is the right call versus Managed Instance, grounded in what the Marketplace wizard exposed.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Deploying Azure SQL: write a one-page deployment recommendation memo for a hypothetical client with 3 different workloads (a small departmental app, a 2TB line-of-business database needing SQL Agent and cross-database queries, and a legacy app requiring OS-level access) — recommending Azure SQL Database, Managed Instance, or SQL Server on a VM for each, with the purchasing model/tier and one sentence of justification per workload.
slots.deliverable: A one-page deployment memo recommending the correct Azure SQL deployment option and tier for each of the 3 hypothetical workloads, with justification.

lessons.title: Choosing the Correct Azure SQL Solution for Business Requirements

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-paragraph recommendation for which Azure SQL solution fits a 10TB reporting database with unpredictable query bursts (Hyperscale vs. General Purpose vs. Managed Instance); then on your AdventureWorksLT database, create a partitioned table manually (partition function + scheme) over a date column, insert sample rows spanning 3 partitions, and query sys.partitions to confirm rows landed in the correct partitions.
slots.deliverable: A written solution recommendation for the 10TB scenario, plus a working partitioned table in AdventureWorksLT with sys.partitions output confirming correct partition placement.

slots.practicalActivity: On a scratch table in AdventureWorksLT, apply ROW and PAGE data compression (ALTER TABLE ... REBUILD WITH (DATA_COMPRESSION = PAGE)) and compare sp_estimate_data_compression_savings output before and after; then design (on paper, not deployed) a horizontal sharding scheme for a hypothetical 500-million-row Orders table split across 4 databases by CustomerID range, documenting your shard key and routing logic.
slots.deliverable: A before/after compression-savings estimate from sp_estimate_data_compression_savings, plus a written 4-shard horizontal sharding design with the shard key and routing logic documented.

lessons.title: Azure Arc, Hybrid SQL & Azure SQL Database in Microsoft Fabric

slots.practicalActivity: Research Azure Arc-enabled SQL Server (for a hypothetical on-prem instance you'd want Azure-managed) and Azure SQL Database in Microsoft Fabric's Mirroring feature; write a short note explaining, for a company that already has Power BI/Fabric in place, why mirroring an existing Azure SQL Database into Fabric might be preferable to building a separate ETL pipeline.
slots.deliverable: A short written note explaining the business case for Azure SQL Database mirroring into Microsoft Fabric versus a custom ETL pipeline.

lessons.title: SQL Authentication vs. Microsoft Entra Authentication
Configuring Microsoft Entra ID for Azure SQL

slots.practicalActivity: On your Azure SQL server from Chapter 1, open the Microsoft Entra ID admin setting in the Portal and set an Entra ID account as the server's Entra admin; then connect to the database from SSMS once using SQL authentication and once using Microsoft Entra authentication, confirming both connections succeed.
slots.deliverable: A configured Entra ID admin on your Azure SQL server, plus confirmation of two successful SSMS connections — one via SQL auth, one via Entra ID auth.

lessons.title: Server Roles, Database Roles & Object Permissions

slots.practicalActivity: In AdventureWorksLT, create a new login and a corresponding database user, add the user to db_datareader; then create a custom database role usp_reporting_role, GRANT it SELECT on the SalesLT schema, and add your new user to that role instead, documenting the difference between the fixed role and your custom role's scope.
slots.deliverable: A working login/user added to db_datareader, plus a custom database role (usp_reporting_role) with schema-level SELECT granted and the user reassigned to it, with notes on the scope difference.

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the DENY-beats-GRANT precedence demo: add your test user to db_datareader (grants SELECT everywhere), then run an explicit DENY SELECT on one sensitive table (e.g. SalesLT.Customer) for that same user and confirm via EXECUTE AS that the DENY blocks access despite the role membership; then REVOKE the DENY and confirm access returns through the role alone.
slots.deliverable: A documented before/after EXECUTE AS test proving DENY overrides a role GRANT, and a second test showing access restored after REVOKE.

slots.practicalActivity: Deliberately break a connection 3 ways (wrong password, a login with no database user mapped, and a user with no GRANT on the table being queried), capturing each exact error message in SSMS; then write a one-line diagnosis and fix for each of the 3 failures.
slots.deliverable: 3 documented login/auth/permission failures with their exact error messages and a one-line fix for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Authentication & Authorization: design and implement a complete least-privilege access model for AdventureWorksLT with 3 roles (read-only reporting, read-write order-entry, and a DBA admin role), create the logins/users/roles in SQL, assign the right GRANTs to each, and add one explicit DENY protecting a sensitive column or table from the reporting role.
slots.deliverable: A working 3-role least-privilege security model implemented in AdventureWorksLT, with one explicit DENY protecting sensitive data from the lowest-privilege role, verified with EXECUTE AS tests.

slots.practicalActivity: On your Azure SQL server, open Networking and add a server-level firewall rule allowing only your current public IP, then connect from SSMS and confirm it works; remove the rule temporarily and confirm the connection is refused, then re-add it; separately, create a virtual network and configure a VNet service endpoint for Microsoft.Sql on one subnet.
slots.deliverable: A documented firewall allow/deny test (connection succeeding and failing based on the rule), plus a VNet with a configured Microsoft.Sql service endpoint.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a private endpoint for your Azure SQL server inside the VNet from the previous slot, confirming it gets a private IP from the subnet; then compare the server's Public network access setting (Selected networks / Disabled) against the private endpoint's connectivity, and write a one-paragraph explanation of when you'd disable public access entirely versus leaving it open with firewall rules.
slots.deliverable: A working private endpoint with a private IP assigned, plus a written explanation of when to disable public network access entirely.

slots.practicalActivity: Deliberately misconfigure connectivity 2 ways (remove your IP from the firewall allow-list, then set Public network access to Disabled without a private endpoint) and, for each, capture the exact SSMS connection error; use the Portal's Diagnose and solve problems blade to see what it reports for each failure, then fix both.
slots.deliverable: 2 documented connectivity failures with their SSMS error messages and the Diagnose and solve problems blade's findings, plus confirmation both were fixed.

lessons.title: Always Encrypted & Always Encrypted with Secure Enclaves

slots.practicalActivity: Confirm Transparent Data Encryption is enabled on your AdventureWorksLT database (it's on by default for Azure SQL) via the Transparent data encryption blade, and note the encryption key source; then enable Always Encrypted on one column (e.g. a mock SSN or credit-card column you add to a scratch table) using SSMS's Always Encrypted wizard, and confirm a query against that column without the right keys returns ciphertext, not plaintext.
slots.deliverable: A confirmed TDE status screenshot/note, plus an Always Encrypted column configured on a scratch table with a query proving ciphertext is returned without the client-side keys.

slots.practicalActivity: Apply Dynamic Data Masking to a column (e.g. an email or phone column) in AdventureWorksLT via the Portal's Dynamic Data Masking blade, then query that column as a masked, non-admin user versus as the admin, confirming the masked output differs; separately, implement Row-Level Security on a table using a security predicate function that restricts rows by a SalesPersonID-style column, testing it with two different user contexts.
slots.deliverable: A masked column with before/after query output (masked vs. unmasked), plus a working Row-Level Security policy tested under two different user contexts.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the Portal's Data Discovery & Classification scan on AdventureWorksLT, review its suggested sensitivity labels, and accept or adjust labels on at least 3 flagged columns; then enable SQL Auditing to a storage account, generate some sample query activity, and review the audit log entries it captured.
slots.deliverable: 3 columns with confirmed or corrected sensitivity classification labels, plus a reviewed SQL Audit log showing captured query activity.

slots.practicalActivity: Enable Ledger on a new table in AdventureWorksLT (or a scratch database) and make a few inserts/updates, then query the ledger's history view to confirm every change is tracked immutably; separately, enable Change Tracking on an existing table and verify CHANGETABLE(CHANGES ...) correctly reports your test modifications.
slots.deliverable: A ledger-enabled table with its history view confirming tracked changes, plus a Change-Tracking-enabled table with CHANGETABLE output verified against real test modifications.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Data Security & Compliance: layer 3 of this chapter's controls onto one sensitive table in AdventureWorksLT — classify its sensitive columns, apply Dynamic Data Masking to at least one, and enable Row-Level Security so a test non-admin user only sees their own rows and sees masked values on the sensitive columns — verified end-to-end with EXECUTE AS.
slots.deliverable: One table with classification, masking, and row-level security all layered together, verified with an EXECUTE AS test showing the restricted, masked view a non-admin user actually sees.

lessons.title: Understanding Database Monitoring & Creating a Performance Baseline

slots.practicalActivity: Run a deliberately heavy query (a cross join or large aggregate) against AdventureWorksLT to generate load, then open Azure Monitor Metrics for the database and chart DTU/CPU percentage, Data IO percentage, and Log IO percentage over the window covering your test query; create a metric alert rule that fires if CPU percentage exceeds 80% for 5 minutes.
slots.deliverable: An Azure Monitor metrics chart showing the resource spike from your test query, plus a working metric alert rule configured at an 80% CPU threshold.

slots.practicalActivity: Open Database Watcher (or, if not available in your subscription, the closest equivalent monitoring dashboard) for your server and explore its fleet-level health view; then run 3 DMV queries DBAs use daily — sys.dm_exec_requests, sys.dm_exec_sessions, and sys.dm_db_resource_stats — against AdventureWorksLT and interpret each result set's key columns.
slots.deliverable: Notes from exploring the fleet-level monitoring view, plus 3 executed DMV queries with a one-sentence interpretation of each result set.

lessons.title: Monitoring Sessions, Connections, CPU, Memory, I/O & Storage

slots.practicalActivity: Create an Extended Events session that captures sql_statement_completed events for AdventureWorksLT, run it while executing a few test queries, and review the captured events in the Watch Live Data viewer; then use sys.dm_exec_connections and sys.dm_os_performance_counters to inspect current sessions and CPU/memory/I/O counters.
slots.deliverable: A working Extended Events session with captured live query events, plus DMV output showing current sessions and CPU/memory/I/O counters.

lessons.title: Reading Execution Plans for Performance Problems

slots.practicalActivity: Apply a structured troubleshooting methodology (baseline, isolate, hypothesize, test, verify) to a slow query you write against AdventureWorksLT's SalesLT.SalesOrderDetail; capture its Actual Execution Plan and identify the single most expensive operator by percentage cost.
slots.deliverable: A documented troubleshooting pass on one slow query, with its execution plan's most expensive operator identified by cost percentage.

lessons.title: Index Seeks, Scans, Lookups & Common Plan Operators

slots.practicalActivity: In the execution plan from the previous slot, identify whether each major operator is a Seek, Scan, or Lookup, and explain why; then run the missing-index DMV query (sys.dm_db_missing_index_details joined to sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats) against AdventureWorksLT and create one suggested index, re-running your slow query to confirm the plan improved.
slots.deliverable: A written seek/scan/lookup breakdown of the plan's operators, plus a missing-index DMV result, a created index based on it, and a before/after plan comparison showing improvement.

lessons.title: Using Query Store to Find Regressed Queries

slots.practicalActivity: Confirm Query Store is enabled on AdventureWorksLT and check its retention settings, run a mix of queries over a few minutes to populate it, then open the Top Resource Consuming Queries report; use the Regressed Queries report to find (or deliberately induce, via a forced bad plan) a query whose performance degraded and force an older, better plan.
slots.deliverable: A Query Store Top Resource Consuming Queries report reviewed, plus a Regressed Queries case where you forced a better historical plan.

slots.practicalActivity: Open two SSMS sessions against AdventureWorksLT: in session 1, start a transaction that updates a row and don't commit; in session 2, try to update or select the same row and observe the block; use sp_who2 and sys.dm_tran_locks to identify the blocking session ID and lock type, then commit session 1 and confirm session 2 unblocks; separately, deliberately create a deadlock between two sessions updating rows in opposite order and capture the deadlock graph.
slots.deliverable: A documented blocking scenario with the blocking session ID and lock type identified via sys.dm_tran_locks, plus a captured deadlock graph from a deliberately induced deadlock.

slots.practicalActivity: Run sys.dm_exec_query_stats joined to sys.dm_exec_sql_text to find your top 5 highest-total-worker-time queries in AdventureWorksLT; then check the database's compatibility level and review an execution plan for a batch-mode or memory-grant-feedback indicator, explaining in a sentence what automatic tuning recommendation (if any) the database currently has pending.
slots.deliverable: A top-5 resource-consuming-query report from DMVs, plus a written note on the database's current Intelligent Query Processing / automatic tuning status.

slots.practicalActivity: Take the single worst-performing query you've found anywhere in this chapter's exercises and tune it end-to-end: capture baseline STATISTICS IO/TIME, identify the plan problem (missing index, non-SARGable predicate, or bad cardinality estimate), apply exactly one fix, and re-measure to quantify the improvement in logical reads and CPU time.
slots.deliverable: A before/after tuning report for one real query: baseline STATISTICS IO/TIME, the specific fix applied, and the measured improvement.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Query Performance Tuning: given 3 slow queries against AdventureWorksLT (one with a missing index, one with a non-SARGable WHERE clause, one causing blocking), diagnose and fix each one using the techniques from this chapter — execution plans, missing-index DMVs, Query Store, and sys.dm_tran_locks — and write a one-paragraph tuning report per query.
slots.deliverable: 3 fixed queries (missing-index, non-SARGable, and blocking cases) each with a one-paragraph written tuning report documenting the diagnosis and fix.

slots.practicalActivity: Run sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats against AdventureWorksLT to find the most fragmented index, then rebuild or reorganize it based on the fragmentation percentage (>30% rebuild, 5-30% reorganize) and re-run the DMV to confirm fragmentation dropped; separately, run UPDATE STATISTICS on a heavily-modified table and compare sys.dm_db_stats_properties' last-updated timestamp before and after.
slots.deliverable: A before/after fragmentation report from sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats showing a successful rebuild/reorganize, plus a before/after statistics-update timestamp comparison.

slots.practicalActivity: Run DBCC CHECKDB on AdventureWorksLT and review its output for any integrity errors; then review and document 3 current database-scoped configuration settings (e.g. MAXDOP, query optimizer compatibility level, parameter sniffing) via sys.database_scoped_configurations, changing one and confirming the change took effect.
slots.deliverable: A clean DBCC CHECKDB run reviewed and documented, plus one database-scoped configuration setting changed and confirmed via sys.database_scoped_configurations.

slots.practicalActivity: Configure Resource Governor (on a SQL Server VM or local SQL Server instance, since Resource Governor isn't available on Azure SQL Database) with a custom resource pool and workload group limiting a simulated reporting workload to 20% CPU, then run a CPU-heavy query under that workload group and confirm the cap holds; separately, on your Azure SQL database, scale compute up one tier and observe the before/after DTU/vCore percentage during a repeated load test.
slots.deliverable: A working Resource Governor pool/workload-group capping a test workload at 20% CPU, plus a before/after resource-utilization comparison from scaling your Azure SQL database's compute tier.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Database Performance & Maintenance: build a single maintenance script for AdventureWorksLT that checks index fragmentation and rebuilds/reorganizes as appropriate, updates statistics on tables with high modification counts, and runs DBCC CHECKDB — then run it and review its full output.
slots.deliverable: One consolidated maintenance script (fragmentation check + rebuild/reorganize, statistics update, DBCC CHECKDB) executed successfully against AdventureWorksLT with its output reviewed.

slots.practicalActivity: On a SQL Server instance with SQL Server Agent available (a VM or local instance, since Agent isn't available on Azure SQL Database), create a new Agent job with 2 steps — one T-SQL step running your Chapter 9 maintenance script, one step logging a completion message — and a daily schedule at a specific time; run it manually once to confirm both steps succeed.
slots.deliverable: A working 2-step SQL Server Agent job with a daily schedule, successfully run manually with both steps confirmed to have succeeded.

slots.practicalActivity: Configure a SQL Server Agent Alert that fires on a specific error severity (e.g. severity 16+) and an Operator with your email, then deliberately trigger a qualifying error to confirm the alert notifies the operator; separately, cause one Agent job step to fail on purpose (e.g. reference a nonexistent table) and use Job History/Activity Monitor to diagnose exactly which step failed and why.
slots.deliverable: A confirmed Agent alert-to-operator notification triggered by a real error, plus a documented job-failure diagnosis using Job History.

lessons.title: Building a DBA Maintenance & Monitoring Strategy

slots.practicalActivity: Automate your Chapter 9 maintenance routine as a recurring SQL Server Agent job on a weekly schedule, with failure notifications wired to your operator from the previous slot; then write a one-page DBA maintenance and monitoring strategy document covering what runs daily/weekly, what alerts exist, and who gets notified.
slots.deliverable: A scheduled, notification-wired recurring maintenance Agent job, plus a one-page written DBA maintenance and monitoring strategy document.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for SQL Server Agent & Automation: build a complete automated maintenance pipeline from scratch — a multi-step Agent job covering index maintenance, statistics, and integrity checks, a weekly schedule, an alert tied to job failure, and an operator who gets notified — then deliberately break one step to confirm the whole alerting chain actually fires end-to-end.
slots.deliverable: A complete, tested automated maintenance pipeline (job + schedule + alert + operator) with a documented end-to-end failure-notification test.

lessons.title: Azure CLI & PowerShell for Database Administrators

slots.practicalActivity: Using Azure CLI or PowerShell (Az module), script the creation of a new Azure SQL database on your existing server (az sql db create or New-AzSqlDatabase), including setting its service tier; run the script twice against two different database names to prove it's repeatable, then delete both via script.
slots.deliverable: A working CLI/PowerShell script that creates an Azure SQL database with a specified tier, run successfully twice against different names and then cleaned up via script.

lessons.title: ARM Templates & Bicep for Azure SQL

slots.practicalActivity: Write a Bicep (or ARM JSON) template that deploys an Azure SQL server and database with parameters for server name, admin login, and tier, then deploy it with az deployment group create and confirm the resource appears in the Portal; separately, research Elastic Jobs' current Azure SQL support and document the use case for running one T-SQL script across every database in an elastic pool.
slots.deliverable: A working Bicep/ARM template deployment creating an Azure SQL server and database via the CLI, plus a documented Elastic Job use case and setup steps.

slots.practicalActivity: Extend your Bicep template from the previous slot to also create a metric alert resource (CPU > 80%) as part of the same deployment, then deliberately pass an invalid parameter (e.g. a duplicate server name) to the deployment to observe and document the exact error Azure Resource Manager returns, and fix it.
slots.deliverable: An extended Bicep template that deploys both the SQL resource and its alert rule in one deployment, plus a documented deployment error and its fix.

lessons.title: Planning a SQL Server Migration to Azure

slots.practicalActivity: Run Microsoft's Data Migration Assistant (DMA) against a local SQL Server instance (or a restored copy of AdventureWorks2012) targeting Azure SQL Database as the destination, reviewing its compatibility and feature-parity assessment report in full; write a one-page migration plan based on what it flagged.
slots.deliverable: A completed Data Migration Assistant assessment report for a real database, plus a one-page written migration plan addressing its flagged issues.

lessons.title: Migrating SQL Server to Azure SQL Database

slots.practicalActivity: Compare the online vs. offline migration options the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) offers for your assessed database, documenting the expected downtime for each; then actually migrate a small database to Azure SQL Database using the Export/Import (.bacpac) method via SSMS, confirming row counts match pre- and post-migration.
slots.deliverable: A written online-vs-offline downtime comparison for DMS, plus a completed .bacpac migration to Azure SQL Database with matching pre/post row counts confirmed.

lessons.title: Migrating to Azure SQL Managed Instance

slots.practicalActivity: Research the additional steps Managed Instance migration requires beyond a single-database migration (network/subnet prep, longer cutover window) and document them; then, on your migrated database from the previous slot, run a post-migration validation checklist — row counts, a sample of business queries returning expected results, and a check of any SQL Agent jobs or linked servers that didn't carry over automatically.
slots.deliverable: A written note on Managed Instance migration's extra requirements, plus a completed post-migration validation checklist with documented results.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Database Migration to Azure: run a full migration simulation end-to-end on a throwaway database — assess it with DMA, choose and justify online vs. offline, execute the migration via DMS or .bacpac, and complete the post-migration validation checklist — writing a short migration runbook documenting every step for a future repeat.
slots.deliverable: A completed end-to-end migration (assessment, execution, validation) on a throwaway database, plus a written migration runbook documenting the steps.

lessons.title: SQL Server Backup Fundamentals: Full, Differential & Log
Backup & Restore with SSMS and T-SQL

slots.practicalActivity: On a local/VM SQL Server instance, take a full backup, make some changes, take a differential backup, make more changes, take a log backup, then restore the full+differential+log chain to a point just before the last change using SSMS's restore wizard and T-SQL RESTORE commands side by side.
slots.deliverable: A completed full+differential+log backup chain restored successfully via both the SSMS GUI and raw RESTORE T-SQL commands, with the restored data confirmed correct.

slots.practicalActivity: On your Azure SQL database, open the Backups blade to review the automated backup schedule and current retention window; then use the Portal's Restore button to perform a point-in-time restore of AdventureWorksLT to a timestamp from earlier today, confirming the restore creates a new database rather than overwriting the original.
slots.deliverable: A reviewed automated-backup configuration, plus a completed point-in-time restore producing a new, separate database confirmed to match the earlier timestamp's data.

lessons.title: Backup to Azure Storage & Disaster Recovery Scenarios

slots.practicalActivity: Configure Long-Term Retention (LTR) on your Azure SQL server with a weekly backup retained for at least 1 month, then review the Portal's Manage backups blade to confirm the LTR policy is active; separately, research configuring backup storage redundancy to geo-redundant storage and write a one-paragraph disaster-recovery scenario explaining how an LTR backup in a different region would be used if the primary region became unavailable.
slots.deliverable: A configured Long-Term Retention policy confirmed active in the Manage backups blade, plus a written geo-redundant-backup disaster-recovery scenario.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Backup & Restore: simulate a real incident — delete a few rows from AdventureWorksLT (or drop the whole database to test the server-level deleted-database restore path), then recover using the appropriate restore method, verify the recovered data matches expectations, and write an incident report documenting detection, restore method chosen, and recovery time.
slots.deliverable: A completed incident-recovery drill (row-level or full-database deletion restored successfully), plus a written incident report covering detection, restore method, and recovery time.

lessons.title: RPO & RTO — Designing from Business Requirements

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-paragraph explanation distinguishing HA from DR using a real example (a failed disk vs. a regional outage); then, for a hypothetical e-commerce database, define concrete RPO and RTO targets (e.g. RPO of 5 minutes, RTO of 1 hour) and name one Azure SQL HA/DR feature from this chapter that could realistically hit each target.
slots.deliverable: A written HA-vs-DR explanation with a real example, plus concrete RPO/RTO targets for a hypothetical database mapped to a specific Azure SQL feature that could meet each.

slots.practicalActivity: Research Always On Availability Groups' architecture (primary + secondary replicas, listener, synchronous vs. asynchronous commit) and diagram a 2-node AG for a hypothetical production database, labeling the listener and commit mode; separately, research Failover Cluster Instances' shared-storage model and write a one-paragraph comparison of when you'd choose an FCI over an AG.
slots.deliverable: A labeled 2-node Availability Group architecture diagram, plus a written FCI-vs-AG comparison paragraph.

slots.practicalActivity: On your Azure SQL database, configure Active Geo-Replication to a secondary region, confirm the secondary shows as 'Readable secondary' in the Portal, and run a read-only query against it; then convert that same setup (or a new database) to use a Failover Group instead, and perform a manual failover, confirming the listener endpoint now points to what was the secondary region.
slots.deliverable: A working geo-replicated secondary confirmed readable, plus a completed Failover Group manual failover with the listener endpoint confirmed to have switched regions.

slots.practicalActivity: Research Log Shipping's architecture for a hybrid scenario (on-prem primary shipping logs to an Azure VM secondary) and diagram the primary/monitor/secondary roles; then, using the Failover Group from the previous slot, run a monitoring/testing drill — check replication lag in the Portal, deliberately fail over, time how long it took, and fail back — documenting the measured RTO against your earlier RPO/RTO targets.
slots.deliverable: A labeled Log Shipping hybrid architecture diagram, plus a documented failover/failback drill with a measured RTO compared against your earlier RPO/RTO targets.

slots.practicalActivity: Project Phase 1: take on the role of DBA for a hypothetical company's legacy on-prem SQL Server environment (use your Chapter 1 AdventureWorksLT database as the stand-in legacy system) — write a short project brief defining the environment and goals, then execute the migrate-and-secure phase: migrate it to Azure SQL Database using Chapter 12's method, configure Entra ID authentication, apply least-privilege roles from Chapter 4, and lock down networking per Chapter 5.
slots.deliverable: A written project brief, plus a migrated Azure SQL database with Entra ID auth, least-privilege roles, and network security controls all applied and verified.

slots.practicalActivity: Project Phase 2: apply Chapter 8/9's performance-tuning and maintenance techniques to your migrated project database (baseline it, fix at least one real performance issue, set up index/statistics maintenance), then automate that maintenance using Chapter 10/11's Agent job or Azure Automation approach, documenting the before/after performance improvement.
slots.deliverable: A documented performance fix with before/after measurements, plus an automated, scheduled maintenance routine for the project database.

slots.practicalActivity: Project Phase 3: apply Chapter 13/14's backup and HA/DR techniques to the project database — confirm automated backups and retention are correctly configured, set up a Failover Group or geo-replication secondary, then run a disaster simulation (force a failover and a point-in-time restore) and write a post-incident report documenting what happened, the recovery time achieved, and whether it met your Chapter 14 RPO/RTO targets.
slots.deliverable: A completed disaster simulation (forced failover + point-in-time restore) on the project database, plus a post-incident report evaluating the result against RPO/RTO targets.

lessons.title: DP-300 Complete Exam Review & Practice Assessment

slots.practicalActivity: Take a full-length DP-300 practice assessment (Microsoft Learn's official practice assessment or an equivalent reputable question bank), score yourself by domain (Plan and implement data platform resources; Implement a secure environment; Monitor and optimize operational resources; Optimize query performance; Automate tasks), and for each domain scoring below 70%, re-do one hands-on exercise from the matching chapter of this course.
slots.deliverable: A scored DP-300 practice assessment broken down by domain, plus a list of which chapter exercises you redid for any domain scoring below 70%.

slots.practicalActivity: Prepare for an Azure DBA interview: write out full answers (not bullet points) to 5 realistic interview questions spanning this course — e.g. 'walk me through migrating an on-prem database to Azure SQL,' 'how would you diagnose a blocked query in production,' 'explain DTU vs. vCore to a non-technical stakeholder' — then do a mock interview out loud (recorded or with a study partner) answering all 5 without reading your written answers.
slots.deliverable: 5 fully written-out interview answers covering migration, performance troubleshooting, and Azure SQL concepts, plus confirmation a spoken mock-interview run-through was completed.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can deploy, secure, monitor, tune, back up, and fail over a real Azure SQL environment end-to-end, and can speak to DP-300 exam domains and real Azure DBA interview questions with hands-on experience behind every answer.
